tagline.text: A small Batanes island where Ivatan stone houses live on

location.label: Location
location.text: Sabtang, Batanes (across the sea south of Ivana Port on Batan Island)

children.text: Sabtang lies a boat ride of
30–45 minutes

from Batan Island, and its Ivatan stone houses of limestone and coral still form living villages. In a single day you can see the stone-house villages of Chavayan and Savidug, vakul weaving, cliff viewpoints and arch rocks.
Sabtang is a small island, the southernmost of the three inhabited islands of Batanes, the northernmost province of the Philippines. Most islanders live in six villages, and in the
census the municipality had 1,774 residents. A paved road loops around the coast, so a tricycle can cover most of the island in half a day.
What made the island famous is its stone houses. The Ivatan built walls of cut limestone blocks and coral stone bound with lime mortar, in places about
1 m

thick. The thick cogon-grass roofs were designed to withstand typhoons and earthquakes. The two typical forms are the maytuab, with a four-sided sloping roof, and the sinadumparan, with stone gable walls at both ends. Chavayan and Savidug keep these houses most intact, and the provincial government has designated both as cultural zones.
Sabtang's recorded history begins with the Spanish missions. Dominican missionaries arrived on the island in the
and built a church, and in

a local uprising led by Aman Dangat is said to have taken place. Traces of far earlier times remain too: in Savidug stands the idjang, the remains of an old fortress built of stacked stones on a rocky hill. In Chavayan, the weavers' association still makes and sells the vakul, a palm-fibre headdress worn by women.
To avoid repeating the overview of
Batanes

, this entry focuses on what to see on Sabtang and how. It suits travelers interested in stone-house architecture, traditional crafts and photography. Be aware, though, that the boat to the island runs only once in the early morning and does not sail at all when the waves are high, so do not plan too tightly.

blocks.title: Chavayan stone-house village and vakul weaving

children.text: Chavayan, at the southern end of the island, is a village of stone houses lined up along both sides of a stone-paved lane. It has the Santa Rosa de Lima chapel, which has kept its cogon roof, and at the weavers' association you can watch vakul being woven. Souvenir vakul are quoted at about
depending on size.

Savidug, on the east of the island, is a village of stone houses along wide lanes, with the Chapel of St. Thomas Aquinas. On a triangular rocky hill behind the village stands the idjang, a pre-Spanish fortress site, introduced as one of the 17 idjang remaining in Batanes.

This cliff viewpoint lies on the road to Chavayan. A small sandy beach is tucked between steep green cliffs, and on clear days you can see islands far across the sea. Many spots have low or no railings, so check the wind before you stand near the edge.

blocks.title: Morong Beach and the Nakabuang arch rock

children.text: On one side of a white sand beach stands a round arch rock carved by wind and waves. Locals call it the Nakabuang or Ahaw arch, and it is often the lunch stop on Sabtang tours. Next to the beach there is also the low-ceilinged Nakabuang cave.
This lighthouse, about

tall, stands on a headland on the Malakdang side near the port. It has long guided ships passing these waters, and with the sea and the grassy headland in one frame it is counted among the best sunrise and sunset photo spots.

blocks.title: San Vicente Ferrer Church and Sinakan

children.text: In Sinakan, the administrative center, stands San Vicente Ferrer Church, said to have been founded by the Dominicans in
. Its white Baroque-style facade and the memorial marker in the front yard are neat and simple, and the church is the heart of island life.

Sumnanga is a small fishing village where stone walls overlap up the hillside. Because of the steep terrain the houses sit in tiers, which has earned it the nickname "Little Hong Kong." The lanes are narrow but paved, and worth a slow stroll.

blocks.title: Wakay Beach and the Malakdang coast

children.text: On the Savidug side, Wakay Beach is a shore where roughly carved rocks catch the eye before any sand. The Malakdang coast has a small cove and sandy beach formed among rocks, a quiet place to rest. On days with big waves, stay out of the water and enjoy the view only.

Staying on the island lets you see the quiet village after the group tourists have left. Rooms are few, so contact your lodging in advance.

Sabtang has no airport, so you must first land at Basco Airport (BSO) on Batan Island. Direct flights from Manila may not operate in some seasons, so the route most reliably described at present is to take a P2P bus from Manila to Clark International Airport (about
2.5–3 hours
) and then fly Clark–Basco. The flight takes about
1 hour 15 minutes
, and fares vary greatly by season.
Details on flight routes and fares are in the
Batanes
entry. Routes change often, so always check the airline's latest notice before booking.
Boats for Sabtang leave from Ivana Port in the south of Batan Island. From Basco town to Ivana is about
20 km
, which takes
30–45 minutes
by tricycle or van. A round-trip tricycle hire has been quoted at about
, and a shared ride at about
one way. To catch the boat you must leave before dawn, so it is safest to arrange your driver the day before.
The boats between the islands are faluwa, traditional vessels without outriggers. They leave Ivana early in the morning (between
) and take about
30–45 minutes
to reach Sabtang port. The fare is quoted at about
one way, though some recent guides give
. Return boats generally run between
8 a.m.
and
, and in the afternoon they sometimes stop early because the waves rise.

The latest information on boat operations from Batan must be checked. Several operators are said to run the route, and departure times and fares change with weather and season. On days when the waves are high the boat does not sail at all, and there is no alternative. Confirm the day before with your lodging, travel agency or operator whether the boat will go.
Tricycles wait at Sabtang port. A hire around the whole island starts at about
for two people, and according to 2025–2026 guides it ranges up to about
. You can also rent a motorbike, but strong winds on the coastal road make it unsuitable for beginners.
From
, visitors to Batanes must register on the online pre-registration portal and pay about
(an ecotourism fee of
plus a visitor ID fee of
). Registration asks you to choose a Department of Tourism-accredited operator, and guidance differs on how far independent travel is allowed, so check the latest notice.
The most comfortable time to see Sabtang is
March–May
, when the sea settles. The waves begin to ease from
February
, and
April
is the driest month and the one when boats are most likely to run. On the other hand, this is peak season, so flights and rooms fill quickly. Daytime temperatures stay around
all year, and annual rainfall is about 1,900 mm.
June
to
November
is typhoon season. In
August
in particular, both flights and the Sabtang boat are often cancelled. From
November
to
February

the northeast monsoon (amihan) blows, bringing cool, windy weather, and on days of rough seas you cannot reach the island. Whatever the season, build into your plans that Sabtang can be reached only on days when the boat runs.

items.label: Island accommodation
items.note: Homestay basis; stone-house stays cost more

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may change depending on local conditions.
On the island, homestays and small lodgings are scattered through Sinakan, Chavayan, Malakdang and elsewhere, quoted at around

per night. Rooms are few, and air-conditioning and breakfast vary by lodging, so check when you book. Staying in a traditional stone house in Chavayan is considered the highlight of a stay here, but such lodgings are few. Most visitors stay in Basco on Batan and cross for the day.

Food centers on Ivatan home cooking. Typical dishes include uvud (minced banana stem), dibang (dried flying fish), lunis (Ivatan-style braised pork) and yellow rice colored with turmeric. Eateries near the port and by Morong Beach feed the day-trippers at lunch. Few long-established eateries could be confirmed, so none are named here; it is easiest to ask your tour operator or lodging to arrange lunch in advance. A self-service souvenir shop near the port is also reported. Coconut crab has declined from overharvesting, so it is best not to order it.
Complete the Batanes online registration before you leave and save your QR code. The fees and procedure must be checked against the latest notice.
The island is reported to have no banks or ATMs. Bring plenty of cash, including for the environmental fee, lunch and souvenirs.
Pack light before boarding. The faluwa rocks a lot and the footing when boarding is narrow.
Treat about
as the last safe time for the return boat when planning. If you are late you may have to stay on the island.
The stone-house villages are places where people live. Ask permission before taking photos, and do not enter a house without permission.
Buying a vakul from the weavers' association helps the makers directly. Ask the size and price first.
There is almost no shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and one extra layer.
Phone signal is weak in some parts of the island. Download maps in advance.

The boat from Batan to Sabtang does not sail when the waves are high, and there is no other way across. If this coincides with flight cancellations you can be stranded for days, so leave slack before your departure home.
During typhoon season (
June
November
), cancellations just before departure are frequent. Prepare travel insurance and a spare budget.
Cliff viewpoints and coastal rocks often have no railings or are slippery. On windy days, stay away from the edge.
Waves and rip currents can be rough along shores such as Morong Beach, so ask locals whether swimming is possible.
The idjang site and old stone houses are heritage in character. Do not move stones, climb on them or write graffiti.
Environmental fees, registration fees and the extent of independent travel change often. Always check the latest guidance before departure.
The gateway to Sabtang. It is about
20 km
from Basco to Ivana Port, and with the Honesty Coffee Shop, churches and grassy hills it is usually visited just before or after a Sabtang trip.
A small uninhabited island in the sea west of Sabtang, a grassy island where cattle and goats graze. It is described as about
15–20 minutes
by boat from Sabtang, and you need to find a boat locally to go there.
The largest island in Batanes, north of Batan Island. It takes about
3–4 hours
by boat from Basco and lies in a different direction from Sabtang, so think of it as a separate trip.
